pages.text: Yellow fever is a viral disease. Most people have fever, chills, loss of appetite, nausea, and headaches. These symptoms usually get better within five days. In some cases, the illness comes back, causing liver damage and yellow skin.
pages.caption: Aedes aegypti feeding

pages.text: The disease is caused by a virus. It spreads through the bite of an infected mosquito. In cities, it spreads mainly through a type of mosquito called Aedes aegypti. This mosquito lives in tropical and subtropical parts of the world.
pages.caption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

imageProvenance.credit: Own scan, slightly modified. Original by Emil August Goeldi (1859 - 1917).

pages.text: A safe and effective vaccine exists to prevent yellow fever. Many countries require travelers to get vaccinated. Other ways to prevent the disease include reducing mosquito populations and diagnosing cases early to stop outbreaks.

pages.text: Yellow fever is common in the tropical areas of South America and Africa, but it does not occur in Asia. Most cases happen in Africa. Since the 1980s, the number of cases has increased because more people live in cities and climates are changing.

pages.text: The disease originated in Africa. It spread to the Americas during the European trafficking of enslaved people. During the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, yellow fever caused major epidemics in many large cities around the world.

Yellow fever is a short viral illness with common early symptoms such as fever, chills, headaches, and muscle pains. While many people improve within five days, about fifteen percent experience a second phase. This severe stage brings abdominal pain, liver damage, and yellow skin.

C1-C2.headline: Epidemiology and Biology of Yellow Fever

pages.text: Yellow fever is an acute viral infection characterized initially by transient symptoms including pyrexia, myalgia, cephalalgia, and emesis. Although a majority of patients experience clinical improvement within five days, approximately fifteen percent progress to a more severe systemic phase marked by hepatocyte damage, jaundice, and elevated hemorrhagic risk.
pages.caption: Aedes aegypti feeding

pages.text: The causative agent is an RNA virus belonging to the genus Orthoflavivirus. Transmission occurs primarily via the vector Aedes aegypti in urban centers across tropical and subtropical zones. Due to clinical similarities with other pathologies, laboratory confirmation via polymerase chain reaction is necessary.
pages.caption: Adults of the yellow fever mosquito A. aegypti: The male is on the left, females are on the right. Only the female mosquito bites humans to transmit the disease.

pages.text: Immunization provides robust prophylaxis, leading many jurisdictions to mandate vaccination for incoming travelers. Vector reduction and early case identification remain critical control measures. Management for infected individuals is exclusively supportive, as specific antiviral interventions are ineffective.

pages.text: Endemic primarily in tropical regions of Africa and South America, the disease accounts for tens of thousands of severe infections annually. Epidemiological tracking indicates an upward trend in incidence since the 1980s, attributed to demographic shifts toward urbanization, heightened human mobility, and environmental alterations favoring vector propagation.

pages.text: Historical records indicate that the disease originated in the African continent, subsequently disseminating to the Americas during the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved populations in the seventeenth century. Throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, yellow fever persisted as a formidable epidemiological hazard, precipitating widespread urban epidemics.
